name: rte_memcpy (DPDK): SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 memcpy for small, cache-resident copies
workload: DPDK's app/test/test_memcpy_perf.c times rte_memcpy against libc memcpy in TSC ticks per copy for sizes up to about 1.5 KB, aligned and unaligned, cache-to-cache, cache-to-memory, memory-to-cache and memory-to-memory, with variable and compile-time-constant sizes; the system-level claim (snippet only) is a vhost Rx/Tx copy path in OvS-DPDK.
claimed_speedup: No rte_memcpy-versus-glibc results are checked into the repo (the test prints a tick pair and a percent difference per size). Intel's article 'Performance Optimization of memcpy in DPDK' (search-result snippet only, page could not be opened): replacing glibc memcpy with rte_memcpy in the DPDK vhost Rx/Tx path gave 22 percent more total bandwidth in a physical-VM-physical OvS-DPDK setup. The 2026 commit d0ab5a7 'eal/x86: optimize memcpy of small sizes' reports only rte_memcpy before/after cycle counts (8 bytes: 4 vs 7 cycles; 16 bytes: 2 vs 4; 64 bytes: 4 vs 7).
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars (GitHub mirror of dpdk.org); core of the DPDK data plane
tradeoffs: Not a libc drop-in: callers use the rte_memcpy() header function. ISA is chosen at compile time from -march macros (SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512); the header forces SSE instead of AVX on GCC older than 11. Tuned for small copies whose source and destination are in cache; large streaming copies are not its target. x86 header plus separate arm/ppc variants.
caveats: The only glibc comparison number (22 percent) is a system-level bandwidth figure from a search snippet of an Intel article that was not opened (intel.com failed with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND here), not a memcpy microbenchmark. The same search surfaced a DPDK mailing-list report (snippet only) that the AVX-512 path was slower than AVX2 in an OvS-DPDK test, and reviewers arguing that constant-size copies are better left to the compiler. The benchmark harness exists in the repo but no CPU, compiler or flags are recorded with any result. last_commit is the date of the latest commit touching rte_memcpy.h (the GitHub commits page for that file), not necessarily the repo head.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'DPDK rte_memcpy AVX512 faster than glibc memcpy small sizes benchmark blog' (Intel developer article, DPDK mailing-list threads); then github.com/DPDK/dpdk, raw test_memcpy_perf.c and rte_memcpy.h, and the commits page of rte_memcpy.h.

name: Vectorized std::search and std::find in the MSVC STL (SSE4.2/AVX2 runtime dispatch)
baseline: MSVC STL's own scalar std::search before vectorization (the same PR also times C strstr as an unchanged control)
workload: benchmarks/src/search.cpp: std::search, ranges::search and default_searcher over a lorem-ipsum haystack with small and large needles near the beginning and end, plus adversarial 'evil' patterns, for uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t and uint64_t elements, timed in ns per search.
claimed_speedup: PR #4745 (1- and 2-byte elements, pcmpestri, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X): classic_search<uint8_t>/0 1976 to 160 ns (12.35x) and /1 2153 to 175 ns (12.30x); classic_search<uint16_t> 4.62x and 4.53x; ranges_search<uint8_t> 9.76x. PR #5484 (32- and 64-bit elements, 5950X): uint32_t 6.95x, 6.23x, 7.61x, 4.23x on the four benign cases; uint64_t 2.88x to 3.03x. Mixed results in the same PR: uint8_t /0 and /1 regressed to 0.78x and 0.76x on the 5950X and the 'evil' uint8_t case ran at 0.33x. In PR #4745 the unchanged C strstr control took 142-143 ns versus 160 ns for the vectorized uint8_t std::search, so strstr stayed faster on those inputs.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (maintainer comment on PRs #4745 and #5484); 12th-gen Intel Core i5-1235U E-cores (contributor run in PR #5484)
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; the standard library shipped with Visual Studio
tradeoffs: x86 and x64 only; SSE4.2 and AVX2 kernels are chosen at run time. Applies only to contiguous ranges of simple element types; per a search snippet of Microsoft's docs the vectorized path sits behind the _USE_STD_VECTOR_ALGORITHMS macro and is separately compiled. Specific to MSVC STL, so libstdc++ and libc++ do not benefit.
caveats: The baseline is the previous scalar std::search, not glibc or std::string::find, and the speedup is a before/after of one library version. Compiler and flags are not stated in the PRs; numbers sit in PR comments rather than a standing results file. Single-byte results are mixed (regressions on the 5950X in PR #5484 and on adversarial inputs), and the bundled strstr control beats the 1-byte vectorized search in PR #4745. Filed here because it is SIMD byte-sequence search in a standard library; the category's std::string::find and memchr/memmem paths were not measured by these PRs. Merged search-related PRs seen: #4654, #4745 (2024-09-09), #5352, #5484 (2025-05-17), #5544.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Microsoft STL vectorized std::find std::search std::count AVX2 speedup devblogs algorithm vectorization'; then github.com/microsoft/STL benchmarks/src and pulls?q=vectorize search merged, PRs #4745 and #5484.

name: Memset by memcpy doubling (riteme gist: 'Memcpy is faster than memset on Intel i7 12700 with glibc 2.36')
workload: Fill a 1 GiB char buffer 100 times with either glibc memset or my_memset, which memsets the first 2 MiB once and then fills the rest by repeatedly memcpy-ing the already-filled block forward.
claimed_speedup: glibc memset 6.34 s elapsed (6.23 s user) versus my_memset 2.57 s elapsed (2.47 s user); the author calls it about 60 percent faster (2.5x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: g++ memset_test.cpp -O3 -march=native (g++ version not stated); -DUSE_MY_MEMSET selects the custom version
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700 (12 cores, 20 threads), 15 GiB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 6.1.0-1, glibc 2.36-6
stars_or_usage: gist with a few comments dated January 2023; last activity 2025-12-27
tradeoffs: A technique snippet, not a library. It only makes sense for very large fills (the first block is memset, the rest is doubled with memcpy), and it needs a correct handling of the final partial block. No licence on the gist.
caveats: Tier A reflects only that code, flags and CPU are stated; the result itself is doubtful. In the gist comments the author's own 'perf bench mem' run on the same i7-12700 shows glibc memset at about 72.7 GB/s versus memcpy at about 31.2 GB/s, which the author calls contrary to the wall-clock test; a commenter on a Ryzen 5700G saw memset and memcpy variants performing similarly; another commenter guesses glibc uses rep stosb for memset and vector moves for memcpy (no disassembly posted). Single wall-clock run, no repetitions, 1 GiB buffer so page-fault and non-temporal-store thresholds may dominate.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch '"faster than glibc" memcpy OR memset OR strlen OR memcmp own implementation blog post github' (gist.github.com/riteme result); then opened the gist.

name: hglm ARM memcpy, memset, memzero and copy_page kernel patches (test-arm-kernel-memcpy)
baseline: original Linux kernel ARM memcpy, memset, memzero and copy_page (the benchmark harness also runs libc memcpy/memset alongside)
workload: bench.script drives benchmark.c over a set of tests (mixed power-of-2 sizes, unaligned mixed sizes, copy_page) for the original kernel routines, libc and the optimized routines on ARMv6 and ARMv7.
claimed_speedup: From the hglm/patches README (page summary): a speedup 'on the order of 70%' for copy_page and larger memcpy on the ARMv6 Raspberry Pi, with a smaller benefit on ARMv7. No results table is checked in for either repo.
hardware: ARMv6 (32-byte cache line, Raspberry Pi) and ARMv7 (64-byte cache line); the README does not name exact SoCs
tradeoffs: 32-bit ARM only (ARMv6/ARMv7); the optimized memcpy, copy_from_user and copy_to_user use PLD unconditionally so they do not work on ARMv4; NEON paths were experimental and later removed from copy_page, memset and memzero; patches no longer applied cleanly to upstream kernels by February 2015.
caveats: First-party claim with a loosely worded 'order of 70%' figure and no stated baseline kernel version, hardware model, compiler or flags. The baseline is the old in-kernel routines rather than glibc, although the harness can compare libc. No licence stated in the pages opened (kernel-derived code is presumably GPL-2.0 but this was not confirmed). Work-in-progress status per the patches README: copy_page, memset and memzero done; memcpy and user-copy variants still in progress.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Raspberry Pi optimised memcpy memset ARM assembly copies-and-fills faster than glibc' returned github.com/hglm/patches; then opened hglm/patches, its arm-mem-funcs directory, hglm/test-arm-kernel-memcpy and raw README.

name: asmlib (Agner Fog): assembly memcpy, memmove, memset, strlen, strcpy and related replacements
baseline: glibc 2.x memcpy, memmove, strlen and other libc string/memory functions (2008-era 32-bit and 64-bit builds)
workload: Fog's own comparisons, posted to the gcc and libc-help mailing lists in July-August 2008, of libc memory and string functions against his asmlib and other 'best function libraries', including memcpy on unaligned data.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippets only (the posts could not be opened): libc 'up to 5 times slower than the best function libraries for important memory and string functions'; libc memcpy 'can be improved by a factor 4-5 for unaligned data on a Core 2'; 64-bit libc still 'better than 32-bit libc but 3-4 times slower' for unaligned operands on an Intel CPU.
hardware: Intel Core 2 for the memcpy claim; other CPUs not stated
stars_or_usage: classic reference library for CPU-dispatched x86 string routines, cited in mailing-list threads and forums
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 only; functions carry an A_ prefix (for example A_memcpy, A_memmove per a PureBasic forum snippet) and the library dispatches on instruction-set level (SSE2 and later), so it is linked or wrapped rather than a transparent libc replacement. Search snippets describe the licence as GPL; the licence file in the zip was not read, so usability is left as reference.
caveats: The repo_url was not opened: www.agner.org, gcc.gnu.org and sourceware.org all failed with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND in this environment, so every number comes from WebSearch snippets of 2008 posts. A glibc developer disputed the comparison in the same thread (glibc 2.6.1 x86-64 routines were already much faster than older glibc). The numbers predate glibc's AVX2 and EVEX ifunc string routines; a masm32 forum snippet shows an asmlib strlen behind other variants on a short-string test, and a forum post says AVX2 assembly gave another 2x over the SSE2 asmlib. No current benchmark of asmlib against modern glibc was found.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Agner Fog asmlib optimized memcpy strlen replacement library faster than glibc' (gcc-list and libc-help 2008 threads, masm32 forum) and 'github asmlib Agner Fog libaes64 libacof64 A_memcpy A_strlen mirror' (PureBasic forum snippet; no GitHub mirror found).

name: arm-mem (bavison): ARM-accelerated memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp and strlen
baseline: generic glibc memcpy, memmove, memset, memcmp and strlen on 32-bit ARM (baseline implied by the description, not named in the README)
workload: No benchmark numbers published; the repo ships a test harness 'inspired by the benchmarker from the pixman library', built with the 'test' make target.
claimed_speedup: No numbers anywhere in the README or in the opened commit messages (NEON strlen and NEON memcmp for Cortex-A53 have title-only messages). The only claim is the description 'ARM-accelerated versions of selected functions from string.h'.
hardware: ARMv6 (-v6l) and ARMv7 (-v7l) builds; NEON strlen and memcmp tuned for Cortex-A53; Raspberry Pi class targets
stars_or_usage: 57 stars; reported (search snippet of a Raspbian package page, not opened) as the source of the Raspbian preload memcpy/memset/memcmp/memmove library
tradeoffs: 32-bit ARM only; strlen exists for ARMv7 only; typically deployed via LD_PRELOAD or linking; NEON variants need NEON. No licence file or licence text on the repo page, so the code cannot be copied.
caveats: Recorded as the single no-numbers entry for this run because it is widely deployed rather than because it has evidence; it has none. The April 2019 'Rewrite memcpy / memmove to tune for Cortex-A53' commit was reverted eleven days later (commit titles), and memcmp return values were fixed afterwards. Related to the already-reported simonjhall/copies-and-fills (Raspberry Pi memcpy/memset), which it is said to descend from in the Raspbian packaging, but that lineage was only seen in a snippet.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Raspberry Pi optimised memcpy memset ARM assembly copies-and-fills faster than glibc' (Raspbian package page snippet naming bavison/arm-mem as source); then github.com/bavison/arm-mem, its commits page and two commit pages.
